ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, W is the endpoint on the left vertical rail, and X is the corresponding endpoint on the right vertical rail; Y and Z are located on the middle vertical axis. Y is connected to the upper central node through a 1 kΩ resistor, and Z is connected on the middle horizontal wire. The diode arrangements and resistor connections on the left and right sides are mirror-symmetric about the Y-Z vertical axis, and below there is also a 1 kΩ resistor connecting the left and right rails. Reasoning: The voltage 1000 sin(omega t) is applied between Y and Z, while both Y and Z are on the axis of symmetry. Since the two left and right half-circuits made of ideal diodes and identical resistors are completely mirror-symmetric, at any instant the sinusoidal voltage will act on the left and right sides in the same way. Therefore the potentials of the mirror nodes W and X are always equal, namely V_W = V_X. So the measured V_WX = V_W - V_X = 0, and this holds for all t.

raw_record.question_text: When a voltage \(1000\sin \omega t\) volts is applied across YZ, what is the voltage measured across WX, assuming ideal diodes?

method.method_draft: First describe the circuit geometry: W and X are mirror-image nodes on the two side rails, while the applied voltage is between the central terminals Y and Z. Because the diode arrangement and resistor values are symmetric with respect to the vertical Y-Z axis, the sinusoidal source drives both halves identically. Therefore the left and right rails must remain at the same potential at every instant, i.e. V_W = V_X. Hence the measured voltage across WX is V_WX = 0 for all t.
